title: No More Fueling Around
summary:
No More Fueling Around
When the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) discusses options for regulating marine emissions of greenhouse gases next week, it will make its case that a single standard is preferable to a patchwork of varying fuel requirements. Whatever plan the IMO eventually produces will join an already‐crowded regime of separate marine fuel regulation that has started to become a more prominent feature in the day‐to‐day tanker market. As if on cue, recent developments in the Mediterranean Aframax market have provided IMO delegates with a clear example of how unevenly enforced marine fuel regulation can have a significant impact on shipping markets.

children.title: The New Rules
children.summary: Since January 1 st 2010, vessels docked in European Union ports for more than two hours while not hooked into shore‐side power have been required to use marine gasoil with no more than 0.1% sulfur to power auxiliary equipment. This requirement is the result of an EU directive published back in 2005, one of several marine fuel regulations to come into force in recent years, summarized in the table below.

children.title: ...More to Come?
children.summary: The EU's new restrictions on marine fuel burned in port and their effect on spot market rates demonstrate that inconsistent enforcement of regulations can have a significant effect on the bottom line. The rules now being more strictly enforced on a selective basis have been known since 2005, allowing plenty of time for ship owners to meet the new regulations.
